name: Wendy Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal day in your accounting firm like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The charity clients upload their files at odd hours, and by morning I am checking receipts against the accounts before the tax return goes to the partner. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification; I know the routine, enjoy explaining a stubborn mismatch to a client, and hate being promised a tidy file that arrives half empty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation, and how do you use AI now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rafael repairs bicycles, and our children Ella and Finn are both school age. We have a mortgage, but I earn higher pay for this job and we have more than a year of expenses saved; plenty of similar firms are nearby. I have never used an AI tool, and I want a clear paper trail and a colleague to check a new method before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little receipt sorter would leave the client calls and return deadlines intact. I could live with that without changing how I check a file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm can use a small tool if it shows where each number came from. I would still want a person to answer a client when a return is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel safe in this picture: my pay is high for this job, we have more than a year of expenses saved, and there are plenty of accounting firms nearby. The mortgage is real, but it is not about to miss a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing the charity accounts and returns with my written checklist. I would add a fixed amount from each monthly wage to our emergency account until it covers fifteen months, rather than spend a bonus before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and bills. A late charity upload still makes me sigh on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the sorter yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, and I would ask our manager Laila for a checked sample before touching it. I would not put a live client file into software just to look agreeable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you add monthly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can move sixty from my pay without touching Rafael’s bicycle-repair income. The extra reserve is new saving for the mortgage, not money already sitting there.

say: I would require **traceable numbers** from any receipt tool.
I would keep a **named accountant** answerable for mistakes.
think: Our **year-long reserve** and high pay keep the mortgage secure.
There are **plenty of firms** nearby if the current office changes.
do: Keep the **written checklist** on charity accounts and returns.
Transfer **sixty monthly** from wages until fifteen months are saved.
S0.quote: A late charity upload still makes me sigh on Friday.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and wants a checked sample before any live file touches it.
Her high salary and **year-long reserve** support a calm baseline and fresh monthly deposits.

steps.text: Keep reviewing charity accounts with written checklist
Transfer sixty monthly from salary until reserve covers fifteen months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first drafts and checks are a lot of my day. I would want to see the staffing sheet before anyone calls the new system a harmless helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our staff council to request a written liability rule and a list of posts the firm plans to fill. I would tell colleagues that a faster return is no gain if a wrong one leaves a client without a person to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my review hours could be reduced when the firm moves checks to software, and a high salary makes my place a target. Our savings give me time to challenge a cut, but Rafael’s bicycle-repair wage alone would not carry our mortgage and two children forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I would bring our current caseload and error records to the staff council and ask it to negotiate notice before hours change. If my paid hours fall in the first year, I would apply only to posted senior accountant jobs with a written wage, hours, and start date that cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, even with a long reserve. I would not treat a job title as security if the actual paid week shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the system to protect your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a live case before an independent error test and paid supervision. I have never used AI, and I would keep my existing review duties while the firm proves the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower wage elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after seeing the full contract and our fixed bills together. I would not resign until a posted job becomes a written offer with an agreed start date.

say: I would seek a **liability rule** and funded staffing list.
I would ask for **notice before hours change** through the staff council.
think: My **review hours** could fall, and my high salary may attract cuts.
Rafael’s repair wage cannot carry our **mortgage and children** indefinitely.
do: Bring **caseload records** to the staff council next week.
Keep current **review duties** while the firm tests the tool.
Apply for **posted senior work** after hour cuts only with written mortgage-covering terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about paid hours despite savings.
S1.quote: I would not treat a job title as security if the actual paid week shrinks.
fieldNote: She grounds collective action in **caseload and error records**, not a vague demand.
Her own **high-paid hours** may shrink; a written offer and agreed date precede any resignation.

steps.text: Bring caseload and error records to staff council for notice terms
Keep reviewing client files under current duties while tool is tested
After first-year hour cuts, take posted senior job with written mortgage-covering wage, hours and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would end before my children leave school. Robots around 2031 would be a second clock for Rafael’s hands-on repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients the firm needs a named signer and a proper route for wrong returns when AGI reaches accounts in 2028. I would ask the staff council to negotiate severance and notice before any desk is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my well-paid review post to go in 2028; Rafael’s bicycle-repair work could face robots around 2031. A year of savings helps, but losing my higher wage while keeping the mortgage would hurt badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would postpone the planned house extension and put its monthly budget into cash, and I would join the staff council’s severance meeting. If my accounting post ends in the first year after 2028, I would accept a posted tax caseworker role only with a written wage, hours, and a start date covering our mortgage and the children’s school schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large wage loss and later risk to Rafael’s work. I can speak up and search. Twelve months of cash is not a lifetime plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rafael about the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Rafael that we can manage in the rooms we have until the income picture is clear. We would not add a renovation loan while both jobs have dates on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a caseworker role be protected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it is also thinking work, and I would treat a real paid opening as a bridge. I would keep my present salary until a signed offer and start date are in hand.

say: I would demand a **named signer** and a route for wrong returns in 2028.
I would seek **severance terms** before staff cuts.
think: I expect my **high-paid review post** to go.
Rafael’s hands-on wage may face **2031 robots** after my desk is hit.
do: Postpone the **house extension** and deposit its monthly cost into cash.
Join the **staff council severance meeting** while still paid.
Take a **posted caseworker role** after layoff only with written mortgage-covering terms.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss.
S2.quote: Twelve months of cash is not a lifetime plan.
fieldNote: Her expected **2028 desk loss** comes before robots could reach Rafael’s bicycle repairs around 2031.
The extension budget becomes **new cash saving**; the caseworker role is a paid bridge, not an assumed refuge.

steps.text: Postpone house extension and deposit its monthly cost into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us negotiate a transition and see which client problems still bring paid work. I would not quit a good wage to test a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff council to seek a funded tax-appeals mentorship and notice before 2031. AGI reaches our accounts desk then, while robots around 2034 are later for Rafael’s hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my current review post could still disappear, but five years lets me learn difficult client appeals while drawing my salary. I have savings, yet I would want a real budgeted opening before claiming a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the council’s paid tax-appeals mentorship only if the firm funds my time and a supervisor is assigned. I would move sixty from each monthly wage into savings; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted appeals post only if its signed pay, hours, and start date cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the future review work, but I have years to see whether the mentorship becomes a paid post. I would keep my current salary if it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mentorship has no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the professional body’s free case notes while continuing the charity returns that pay me now. I would not spend our reserve on a course without a job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the council for anything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a yearly count of posts removed and actual appeals openings. A promise of training means little if every new vacancy is frozen.

I would distinguish **2031 desk loss** from later 2034 robots.

do: Take **paid supervised mentorship** only if the firm funds time and assigns a supervisor.

fieldNote: Her retraining requires **funded paid time** and an assigned supervisor, with free case notes if no place opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would see the children into adult life. I would still want the firm to say plainly what happens to the review desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm has time to protect apprenticeships and keep a human tax-signing rule before AGI reaches desks in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not postpone that screen-work date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect routine preparation fees to fall, but our high pay and year of savings make the next few years secure. I could have a fuller appeals record by 2036 if the firm funds real practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep signing off current charity returns and transfer sixty each month from salary until our reserve covers eighteen months. I would do supervised appeals only if the firm funds paid time; if my review post contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted appeals role only with signed wages, hours, and a start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about what happens later, but not about the next payment. I can set a long plan without telling the children we are safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a legal change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff council to press for a clear human sign-off rule and notice before any automated cut. I would bring real error cases to that meeting, with client names removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children to study accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Ella and Finn to learn how to question an answer, whether from a person or a tool. I would not promise them any single profession will keep the same shape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my well-paid review post to be cut before a new role has a signed contract. Agreed severance, funded supervised appeals practice, and posted vacancies with wages would help. I would use the reserve to search without leaving a current wage on a rumour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays when an automated return is wrong and a small charity gets a penalty. A faster file can be an expensive mistake for a client with no spare cash. I want someone named on the answer.

headlineQuote: A faster file can be an expensive mistake for a client with no spare cash.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who reviews charity returns.
She has **high pay**, more than a year saved, a bicycle-repair partner, two school-age children, and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and wants a paper trail and human accountability for returns.
She brings **caseload evidence** to the staff council before negotiating notice and severance.
The **2028** desk shock alarms her despite savings; a longer warning lets her test funded appeals work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her high-paid review post before a signed replacement role exists.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **severance terms**, funded supervised appeals practice, and posted vacancies with written wages.
